$comment: One row per rule in this repository's contract: what enforces it, what it is currently absorbing, and every breach recorded against it. Kept honest by scripts/contract-ledger.mjs (`npm run contract:ledger:check`, blocking inside check:ci): a rule defined in the sources with no row here fails, and a row claiming a rule that no longer exists fails. Most of the numbers are reporting-rung — they inform what AGENTS.md should say next, they never fail a build. The exception is `ceiling`, below. Breaches are appended by `--record`, fed the JSON a rubric review writes.
$ceiling: A row that measures an EXCEPTION LIST (a SAST allowlist, the names a lint fence waves through) carries `ceiling: { max, reason, comesOffWhen }`, and `--check` fails when the list grows past `max`. Why: both lists are the right shape — narrow, each entry read and accepted — and both are one entry away from being the wrong one, because an exception list that grows a line per inconvenient diff erodes its fence without a build ever going red. `max` is what the list holds today, so this is green on arrival (ADR-0007). `comesOffWhen` is the field an exemption list normally never has, and the reason exemptions become permanent. Raising a ceiling is fine and is the point: it is one reviewed line next to the entry it pays for.
$breaches: Empty for every row today, and that is a statement about the ledger's age rather than about the rules: recorded breaches start accumulating from the first review run that is folded in with `--record`. The 'Absorbing now' column is NOT empty, because absorbed debt (allowlist entries, ratchet baselines, files already over a limit) is measured live from the files the gates read — so this ledger says something useful on the day it lands.

rules.guidance: AGENTS.md § Conventions that bite — a commit subject names the change, not the session
rules.why: the log is what a future agent bisects; 'fix: Done. Here's what I found' is well-formed and useless
a caller that reaches for a driver has picked a backend and skipped the tenant key

ceiling.reason: Nothing has ever been allowlisted against the store seam: every caller reaches data through a store in src/lib, which is where the tenant key is applied. A ceiling of 0 records that, and makes the first exception a diff somebody argues about rather than a line somebody adds.

rules.why: a route that establishes no caller identity mints a phantom tenant instead of failing

ceiling.reason: Five anonymous routes, and each one's caller genuinely cannot sign in: a merchant-feed robot, a webhook from Meta or a mail forwarder, a signed-out visitor on the marketing site, a scan claimed before the sign-in redirect. None is unguarded — each is behind an unguessable 128-bit token in the path, an HMAC over the raw body, or a durable per-IP daily cap, and none spends AI units.
ceiling.comesOffWhen: An entry comes off when its caller gains a real identity: feed/[token] and twin/inbound/[token] when a machine caller can authenticate as the project rather than by holding a URL; images/upload-ref and sken/claim if the marketing site stops serving the signed-out flow they exist for. A sixth entry is not a variation on these — it is a product decision about anonymity, and it belongs in the diff that raises this number.

rules.guidance: AGENTS.md § Security rules are a gate
rules.why: a server env var read in a client module ships to the browser

ceiling.reason: No client module has ever needed a server env var: the shape that works is a server component reading it and passing a value down, and that shape has always been available. A ceiling of 0 keeps 'just this once' from being a one-line edit — the failure mode here is a secret shipped to a browser, which no reason survives.

rules.guidance: AGENTS.md § Security rules are a gate
rules.why: dynamic code execution in a process holding live advertiser credentials

ceiling.reason: Dynamic code execution has never been needed in a process that holds live advertiser credentials, and a model's output is the input most likely to reach one. A ceiling of 0 is the whole rule.

rules.guidance: AGENTS.md § Security rules are a gate
rules.why: SQL built by interpolation; the two exceptions are table NAMES, which cannot be bound

ceiling.reason: Two statements interpolate a table NAME, which SQLite cannot bind as a parameter — a PRAGMA in src/lib/db.ts and a three-table sweep in the leads local store. In both, the name comes from a literal array written inline in the same file and every caller-supplied value in the statement is bound.
ceiling.comesOffWhen: When neither call site needs a dynamic table name — the PRAGMA when the schema check is generated per table, the sweep when leads live in one table. Any third entry is a different claim: it would be the first one where the interpolated value is not a literal from the same file.

rules.why: a credential-shaped identifier passed to console survives in the platform's log retention

ceiling.reason: Nothing credential-shaped has ever had to reach console. Vercel's log retention outlives the incident, so an allowlisted entry here is a secret with a retention policy attached — the fix is always to log the identifier's shape rather than its value.

rules.why: a route importing the decrypted BYOM key can return it by accident

ceiling.reason: One route legitimately holds a decrypted BYOM key: 'test connection' has to call the vendor with it. It is behind requireByomUser and a per-user probe floor, and the key never reaches the response.
ceiling.comesOffWhen: When validation moves behind a lib-side seam that takes the user and returns a verdict, so no module under src/app/api imports the decrypted key at all. A second route needing the plaintext key is the signal to do that, not to add a line here.

rules.why: TLS verification disabled anywhere in a process that talks to ad platforms

ceiling.reason: TLS verification has never been switched off anywhere in this process, and the processes that talk to Google Ads and Sklik are the ones where it would matter most. A local certificate problem is a local problem — it does not earn an entry that ships.

rules.why: a secret-shaped value behind NEXT_PUBLIC_ is a published secret

ceiling.reason: No secret-shaped value has ever been put behind NEXT_PUBLIC_. There is no reason that makes a published secret acceptable, so this ceiling has nothing to trade against — an entry here means the variable was misnamed or the value should not be in the browser.

rules.why: a key-derived cipher with no explicit IV

ceiling.reason: The one thing encrypted here is a user's BYOM key, and it uses an explicit IV. A key-derived cipher with no IV is never the smaller change — it is a rewrite of stored data waiting to happen, so 0 is the only number that keeps that decision out of a hurried diff.

rules.why: the LLM chokepoint and the store seam, refused in the editor rather than in a diff

ceiling.reason: Three names cross this fence, and they are the same name three times: `geminiAvailable`, `claudeAvailable`, `codexAvailable`. Each is a boolean about whether a provider is CONFIGURED — it cannot be used to make a call, which is the thing the fence exists to route through generateStructured().
ceiling.comesOffWhen: When the three probes are re-exported from src/lib/llm/index.ts. Callers would then import the entry point like everyone else and the fence would need no exception list at all. A fourth entry is not another probe — it would be the first symbol that lets a caller do something with a provider, and that is the fence failing, not the list growing.

rules.why: src/lib owns the drivers, so it relaxes the store half — and keeps the chokepoint half

ceiling.reason: The same three availability probes as `adamant/seams`, restated because ESLint merges `no-restricted-imports` by rule id: a narrower block REPLACES the wider one's options rather than adding to them, so the exception list has to be written twice or the chokepoint half is silently dropped for src/lib.
ceiling.comesOffWhen: Together with the copy in `adamant/seams` — re-export the probes from src/lib/llm/index.ts and both lists go to zero. Until then the two counts must move together; one of them growing alone means the fences have drifted apart.

rules.enforcedBy: eslint.config.mjs (the exception the fence is built around)
rules.why: src/lib/llm is allowed to be the exception it enforces on everyone else

ceiling.reason: One waiver: `no-restricted-imports` is off inside src/lib/llm/**, because that directory is the chokepoint — it is where the clients are constructed and the provider order, BYOM keys, demo fallback, metering and telemetry live. A fence has to exempt its own implementation or it cannot be implemented.
ceiling.comesOffWhen: It does not; this one IS the fence's definition. The ceiling is here so a SECOND directory cannot join it quietly — the whole value of a chokepoint is that there is exactly one place the rule does not apply.

rules.why: the editor-time half of A2

ceiling.reason: This fence has no exception list and never needed one: the shape that works under cacheComponents is a <Suspense> boundary around the dynamic read, which is available on every route. `maxDuration` and `preferredRegion` are not exemptions — they were never restricted, because they are Vercel function settings rather than caching opt-outs.

rules.enforcedBy: scripts/actions-pin.mjs — third-party blocking, first-party EXEMPT (STRICT = false)
rules.why: a tag is a mutable pointer; a retagged action runs with the pipeline's token before any downstream proof applies
rules.verdict: green by exemption — the one rule here that passes because it is switched off for the actions this repo actually uses. Closing it is one networked run (`npm run actions:pin`), which no offline session can do.

rules.guidance: AGENTS.md § Two of these are enforced rather than trusted
rules.why: an expression spliced into a run: body is source code, not an argument
parity is the type system; what typecheck cannot see is measured instead of asserted
the checkout is shared with concurrent agents, so `git add -A` commits someone else's half-finished work
rules.verdict: unfenceable from inside this repo (the damage is done by the time a hook sees it), and it has bitten before — the closest thing to a fence is that a commit which breaks the build is the committer's to fix.

rules.id: never raise a ratchet you could have lowered
rules.enforcedBy: nothing — each ratchet enforces its own direction, nothing enforces the intent
rules.why: raising a baseline is how a finding gets absorbed instead of fixed
rules.verdict: candidate fence: three baselines have been raised legitimately (a new AI tool ships unbaked), and nothing distinguishes that from absorbing a regression. A raised baseline could be required to carry a reason in the same commit, the way a golden already is.

rules.enforcedBy: partly the runtime guards (SKLIK_WRITES_ENABLED, the schranka review gate); the boundary itself is prose
